options.link/down: The interface has no link: the cable is out, the port of the switch is down, or the driver stopped.
options.link/flap: The link goes down and comes up again and again.
options.link/corrupt: A bad cable or a bad port damages frames, so the receiver drops them for their checksum.
options.link/rate: The link runs at a low rate, for example 10 Mbit/s after a bad negotiation.
options.link/mismatch: The two ends of the link do not agree on the duplex, so frames collide and drop under load.
options.link/loop: A loop of switch ports with no spanning tree sends broadcast frames around, and they fill the network.
options.link/wrong: The port or the radio puts the client on a wrong network, for example a wrong VLAN.
options.link/exhaust: The MAC table of a switch is full, so the switch sends each frame to each port.
options.link/size: The host sends frames that are larger than a switch of the network carries, and the switch drops them.
options.link/filter: The port of the switch blocks the client, for example after a failed 802.1X sign-in or a port security rule.
options.wifi/down: The access point stops, so the client finds no network.
options.wifi/flap: The client leaves the access point and joins it again and again.
options.wifi/loss: The radio link loses frames: for a weak signal, for other radios on the channel, or for multicast frames only.
options.wifi/delay: The radio of the client or of the access point sleeps to save power, so frames wait.
options.wifi/refuse: The access point refuses the client: a wrong passphrase, a refused 802.1X sign-in, a MAC filter, or a full access point.
options.wifi/rogue: A second access point with the same network name takes the client.
options.ip/down: The part stops: the DHCP server gives no address, or the target host is off.
options.ip/rogue: A second device answers for the real one: a second DHCP server, or false ARP answers for the address of the gateway.
options.ip/duplicate: Two hosts of the link have the same IPv4 address.
options.ip/exhaust: The address pool of the DHCP server is full, so new clients get no address.
options.ip/wrong: The host has a wrong address or a wrong mask, from its own settings or from wrong DHCP options.
options.ip/filter: A filter drops ICMP echo, and the host is up.
options.ip/stale: A neighbor cache keeps an old link address after a device changes, so frames go to the old device.
options.ip/missing: The host has IPv6, and a router on the path has no IPv6 route to the target.
options.route/down: The gateway does not forward packets, and the link stays up.
options.route/missing: No router of the link sends router advertisements, so the host has no IPv6 default router.
options.route/wrong: A route of the host or of the gateway sends packets to a wrong next hop, for example a route that a VPN left.
options.route/rogue: A second device sends router advertisements, so hosts use a wrong default router or a wrong prefix.
options.route/exhaust: The NAT has no free external port, so it drops the first packet of each new flow.
options.route/filter: The NAT does not hairpin, so a host cannot reach a host of its own network through the external address.
options.route/flap: The default route changes again and again, for example when two routers of the link both take the gateway address.
options.path/loss: A congested or damaged link on the path drops a share of the packets.
options.path/delay: The path is long, for example a satellite link or a detour through a far network, so each packet is late.
options.path/jitter: The delay of the packets changes from packet to packet.
options.path/reorder: Packets arrive in a different order, for example over two links of different delay.
options.path/duplicate: A device on the path sends some packets two times.
options.path/corrupt: A device on the path changes bits of the packets, so the receivers drop them for their checksum.
options.path/rate: A slow link or a shaper on the path carries the packets at a low rate.
options.path/queue: A device on the path has a large buffer, so under load its queue stays full and the delay rises.
options.path/size: A link on the path has a small MTU. Alone it is no fault, because Path MTU Discovery finds the size.
options.path/filter: A filter on the path drops a kind of packets: ICMP Packet Too Big messages, or replies that come back on another path.
options.path/down: A route sends the packets of a prefix to a network that drops them, with no ICMP message.
options.path/loop: Routers forward the packets of a prefix in a loop: two static routes send it to each other, or the routes converge after a failure.
options.path/rogue: A different network announces the prefix of the target, so the traffic of the prefix goes to that network.
options.path/wrong: A network passes routes beyond their scope, so traffic goes through a network that cannot carry it.
options.path/flap: A route on the path is withdrawn and announced again and again, so the path changes and drops packets.
options.path/exhaust: The route table of a router on the path is full, so the router drops the packets of the prefixes that it cannot hold.
options.path/missing: A router on the path has no route to the target, and it answers with an ICMP unreachable message.
options.dns/down: The DNS server does not answer: the resolver, the forwarder of the gateway, or each authoritative server of the zone.
options.dns/refuse: The resolver answers with an error for each name, for example when it reaches no authoritative server.
options.dns/missing: The name does not exist, for example after a typing error or a deleted record.
options.dns/wrong: The DNS data is wrong: the parent zone delegates to a server that does not serve the zone, or a record has a wrong address.
options.dns/intercept: A device of the network answers the queries for other resolvers, or it changes their answers.
options.dns/rogue: A false answer gets into the cache of the resolver, so the resolver gives a wrong address for the name.
options.dns/stale: A cache keeps an old record after the zone changes it, until its TTL ends.
options.dns/expire: The DNSSEC signatures of the zone expire, because its signer stopped.
options.dns/mismatch: The DS record of the parent does not match the keys of the zone, so validating resolvers reject its answers.
options.dns/filter: A filter drops DNS traffic: the queries to resolvers outside the network, or DNS over TCP.
options.dns/loss: The resolver drops a share of the queries, so lookups wait for a retry.
options.dns/exhaust: The resolver or the forwarder of the gateway gets too many queries, so it drops or refuses the new ones.
options.dns/skew: The clock of a validating resolver is wrong, so it rejects valid DNSSEC signatures.
options.dns/size: A filter on the path drops IP fragments, so a large DNS answer over UDP does not arrive.
options.dns/loop: Two forwarders send queries to each other, or a chain of aliases comes back to its start.
options.tcp/missing: No program listens on the port, so the host resets the connect.
options.tcp/filter: A firewall drops the packets to the port with no message, or a middlebox drops a SYN with the ECN flags.
options.tcp/refuse: A firewall or a load balancer on the path resets connections that it does not accept.
options.tcp/expire: A NAT or a firewall removes the state of an idle connection before its ends close it.
options.tcp/exhaust: A table is full: the queue of new connections of the server, or the connection table of a NAT or a firewall.
options.tcp/stall: The server or a proxy accepts the connection and then sends nothing.
options.tcp/mismatch: A middlebox removes or changes TCP options, for example the window scale, so the connection is slow or stops.
options.tcp/intercept: A transparent proxy ends the TCP connection and opens its own connection to the server.
options.tls/expire: A certificate of the chain expires: the certificate of the server, or a root that old clients trust.
options.tls/wrong: The server gives a certificate for a different name, a chain with no intermediate certificate, or a chain to a private root. A private root that the clients trust is no fault alone.
options.tls/mismatch: The client and the server have no TLS version or cipher in common.
options.tls/intercept: A device ends the TLS connection and gives a certificate from a root that the clients were made to trust.
options.tls/skew: The clock of the client is wrong, so valid certificates seem not yet valid or expired.
options.tls/filter: A middlebox reads the server name of the handshake, and it blocks or resets the connections to some names.
options.tls/size: A middlebox drops a ClientHello that needs more than one packet, for example with post-quantum key shares.
options.http/intercept: A captive portal holds the traffic and changes the answers until the user signs in.
options.http/delay: The server is slow, so the answer comes late, or a proxy before it times out.
options.http/refuse: The server answers with errors, a proxy of the network fails, or a proxy asks for credentials before it sends requests on.
options.http/stale: A cache or a CDN gives an old version of the page after the server changes it.
options.http/loop: The redirects of the server come back to their start, so the client never gets a page.
options.http/exhaust: The server limits the rate of the client, and it refuses the requests above the limit.
options.http/mismatch: A newer HTTP version fails on the path, for example HTTP/3 when a filter drops UDP, so the client waits before it falls back.
options.http/wrong: A cache or a CDN gives the page of a different site or of a different user.
